title: Air Force One and the Modern Presidency
hook: A historian's argument that the presidency we recognize today — constantly travelling, personally diplomatic, permanently campaigning — was built by an airplane.
key_points: Before jet travel, presidents rarely left Washington; the office was run from one city.
Kennedy's Boeing 707, delivered in 1962, made routine domestic and foreign travel possible.
Presidents could now do official business and campaign on the same trip, fusing governing with electioneering.
Summits and state visits shifted diplomacy from cables and envoys toward the leader in person.
The plane is also a mobile command post — on 9/11 it kept Bush safe, though its comms initially faltered.
content_html: It is easy to read Air Force One as a symbol — a flying set piece, or a piece of expensive hardware to argue about. Historian Peter Kastor makes a stronger claim: the presidency as we know it "would have been impossible without Air Force One." Before jet aircraft, presidents largely stayed in Washington and governed from it. The Boeing 707 delivered for John F. Kennedy in 1962 turned constant movement into a normal condition of the office, and the office reshaped itself around that capability.
extra_html: Writing in The Conversation, Kastor traces three consequences. Domestically, a president could suddenly conduct official business and campaign on the same trip — Bill Clinton visited 37 states in 73 days in his first year — which mattered all the more after the 1970s shift to primary-based candidate selection made incumbent travel essential. Internationally, leadership moved from the desk to the summit: where Roosevelt and Eisenhower coordinated global affairs largely from Washington, Kennedy and his successors placed themselves personally at the center of world events, as with Nixon's 1972 visit to China or Reagan's 1986 meeting with Gorbachev in Iceland. And the plane doubles as a hardened command post, a role visible on September 11, 2001, when it kept President Bush secure even as its communication systems initially faltered and briefly cut him off from Washington. The broader lesson generalizes beyond one country: institutions are shaped not only by constitutions but by the technology available to the people inside them.

related.title: The Executive
related.hook: Laws don't enforce themselves. The executive is the branch that runs the state day to day — carrying out the law, commanding the bureaucracy, and acting in a crisis.

related.title: The Politics of Spectacle
related.hook: Bread and circuses, military parades, staged combat — leaders have always used spectacle to project power and bind people to a shared identity.

related.title: Diplomacy & War
related.hook: States pursue their interests on a spectrum that runs from the conference table to the battlefield. Diplomacy and war are two ends of the same toolkit.

flashcards.prompt: What is the historian's core claim about Air Force One?
flashcards.back_html: That the modern presidency would have been impossible without it — routine travel reshaped how presidents govern, campaign, and conduct diplomacy.

flashcards.prompt: How did presidential air travel change the relationship between governing and campaigning?

choices.text: A sitting president could carry out official duties and campaign on the same trip
It made campaigning illegal while in office
It moved campaigning entirely to television and off the road

flashcards.explanation_html: The plane let incumbents combine the two, which mattered even more after the 1970s shift to primary-based candidate selection.

flashcards.prompt: What does the article say Air Force One changed about diplomacy?

choices.text: Presidents became personally central to world affairs rather than directing them from Washington
It ended the need for ambassadors and treaties
It shifted diplomacy to the legislature

flashcards.explanation_html: Earlier presidents coordinated from Washington; from Kennedy onward, summits and state visits put the president personally at the center.
